The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own

  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a

  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

1	Introduction
     2	 The Apgar score is based on five components (skin color, heart rate, reflex irritability, muscle
     3	tone, and respiration). Each item is scored from 0 to 2 with a total score of 7–10 as normal and the
     4	highest score of 10 representing the optimal condition. The Apgar score has been used worldwide as a
     5	vitality index for almost every newborn immediately after birth.
     6	
     7	
     8	
     9	
    10	 Methods
    11	 Study Population
    12	 We conducted a population-based cohort study using data from Danish national registers. A total of
    13	2,272,473 live singletons were identified during 1978–2015 from the Danish Medical Birth Registry .
    14	We excluded 1,001 births with missing information on sex and 41,252 births with no valid information
    15	on 5-min Apgar scores (including the score of 0). We further excluded 16,398 infants who died or
    16	emigrated from Denmark before the age of 1 year. The final cohort comprised 2,213,822 births.
    17	
    18	
    19	
    20	
    21	 Discussion
    22	 Main Findings
    23	 In this large population-based cohort study, during childhood, we found individuals with even
    24	clinically “normal” Apgar score range of 7–9 still had higher risks of overall mental disorders and
    25	some specific diagnoses: organic disorders and a series of neurodevelopmental disorders
    26	(intellectual disability, pervasive developmental disorders, childhood autism, and ADHD). It is also
    27	interesting to observe that compromised Apgar scores were at elevated risks of developing organic
    28	disorders and neurotic disorders, which were reported for the first time. During early adulthood,
    29	compromised 5-min Apgar scores were not found to be associated with mental disorders.
    30	
    31	
    32	 Comparisons With Other Studies
    33	 To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association of the full spectrum of mental
    34	disorders with the 5-min Apgar score. Our findings indicate the strongest associations for
    35	intellectual disability in childhood, which corroborates the results from previous studies. Most
    36	previous studies were based on results of different non-standardized intelligence tests, and
    37	cross-sectional or descriptive designs, except a recent Swedish study, by virtue of clinically
    38	confirmed diagnosis and cohort design, reporting that term infants with low 5-min Apgar score had a
    39	higher risk of severe neurologic morbidity, including a 9-fold risk of intellectual disability.
    40	However, the Swedish study only captured cases before 14 years of age and only adjusted for year of
    41	birth, maternal age, parity, and smoking. Similarly, we observed 3~5-fold risks of intellectual
    42	disability in childhood (until 18 years of age), and we were able to adjust for not only the
    43	aforementioned confounders but also parental psychiatric history and socioeconomic status,
    44	indicating a more robust association. In addition, ADHD and autism were another two widely studied
    45	neurodevelopment disorders in relation to Apgar score during childhood, but existing results were
    46	inconsistent, which may be due to heterogeneity of methodology, in particular categorizations of
    47	Apgar scores and definition of outcomes. For example, some studies used pervasive developmental
    48	disorder (ICD-10 codes: F84) as a proxy to define autism, which includes but is not limited to
    49	autism. To reduce the possibility of misclassification, we only focused on childhood autism–the
    50	typical and most severe type of autism–to explore the association. Our findings further support that
    51	compromised 5-min Apgar scores were associated with childhood autism.
    52	
    53	
    54	 Furthermore, we observed that individuals with a compromised 5-min Apgar score had higher risks of
    55	organic disorder and neurotic disorder during childhood, which have not been reported previously.
    56	These findings imply that less-than-optimal Apgar scores at birth may be an indicator for a broad
    57	scope of mental disorders in childhood, not merely neurodevelopmental disorders.
    58	
    59	
    60	 There have been scarce studies examining the association between low Apgar score and adulthood
    61	mental health. We did not find that compromised 5-min Apgar scores were associated with mental
    62	disorders during early adulthood, which may be attributed to incomplete records of Apgar scores
    63	during the initial establishment of the Danish Medical Birth Register (MBR). We observed that
    64	participants with suboptimal Apgar scores at 5 min tended to have higher risks of organic disorders,
    65	schizophrenia, neurotic disorders, and personality disorders, and the low statistical precisions may
    66	probably be due to limited cases in the low Apgar score groups. Considering that the maximum
    67	attained age in our study was only up to 39 years, the follow-up between 19 and 39 years was not
    68	long enough to detect some late-onset mental disorders (e.g., dementia), therefore, future studies
    69	with extended follow-up to late adulthood are warranted.
    70	
    71	
    72	 Current guidelines recommend Apgar scores of 7 or higher to be reassuring, hence, infants with
    73	these scores are often assumed to constitute a homogeneous group. Nevertheless, recent studies
    74	showed that even reassuring Apgar scores of 7–9 are associated with higher risks of neonatal
    75	mortality, neonatal morbidity, and adverse long-term neurological outcomes, compared with an Apgar
    76	score of 10. We found a dose-response increasing the overall risk of mental disorders with
    77	decreasing Apgar score of 9 toward 7. Furthermore, individuals with “normal” scores of 7–9 carried
    78	increased risks of a wide range of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as intellectual disability,
    79	pervasive developmental disorders, childhood autism, and ADHD. Similarly, prior studies based on
    80	developmental screening scales found children aged 5 years with 5-min Apgar scores of 7–9 were more
    81	vulnerable on the emotional or physical health domain of the Early Development Instrument. Recently,
    82	a large transnational study also suggested that low Apgar scores of 7–9 were associated with a
    83	higher risk of autistic disorder but without controlling for socioeconomic status and paternal
    84	psychiatric history. Our findings are in line with those of previous studies by showing that
    85	reassuring Apgar scores 7–9 are associated with various neurodevelopmental disorders in childhood.
    86	These findings support that 5-min Apgar scores routinely available in contemporary neonatal
    87	settings, even within the normal range 7–9, are not totally reassuring.
    88	
    89	
    90	 The causes of mental disorders are multifactorial. Adverse prenatal events (e.g., gestational
    91	diabetes mellitus, preterm, and restricted fetal growth) are important risk factors and could have a
    92	programming effect on fetal brain development, resulting in increased risk for psychopathology later
    93	in life. In this study, adjusting for gestational age at birth and fetal growth status did not
    94	substantially change the risks, indicating that preterm birth or restricted fetal growth do not
    95	strongly modify the relations between low Apgar scores at birth and subsequent mental disorders.
    96	Although Apgar scores are not clear on any causal pathway of pathogenesis, less-than-optimal Apgar
    97	scores at birth may be a potential sign of the cumulative effect of those adverse prenatal events.

Based on the article in `doc.txt`, here is an explanation of the Apgar score and what the study found about its significance for health outcomes.

## What the Apgar score is

The article defines it as follows: "The Apgar score is based on five components (skin color, heart rate, reflex irritability, muscle tone, and respiration). Each item is scored from 0 to 2 with a total score of 7–10 as normal and the highest score of 10 representing the optimal condition." It is "used worldwide as a vitality index for almost every newborn immediately after birth."

## The study behind the article

The authors "conducted a population-based cohort study using data from Danish national registers," identifying "2,272,473 live singletons... during 1978–2015 from the Danish Medical Birth Registry," with a final cohort of "2,213,822 births."

## Significance for health outcomes

**Even "normal" scores carry some risk.** The main finding is that "individuals with even clinically 'normal' Apgar score range of 7–9 still had higher risks of overall mental disorders and some specific diagnoses: organic disorders and a series of neurodevelopmental disorders (intellectual disability, pervasive developmental disorders, childhood autism, and ADHD)." The authors note a "dose-response increasing the overall risk of mental disorders with decreasing Apgar score of 9 toward 7."

**Lower scores carry greater risk.** "Compromised Apgar scores were at elevated risks of developing organic disorders and neurotic disorders, which were reported for the first time." The strongest association was for intellectual disability: the authors "observed 3~5-fold risks of intellectual disability in childhood (until 18 years of age)," and their findings "further support that compromised 5-min Apgar scores were associated with childhood autism."

**Early adulthood.** "During early adulthood, compromised 5-min Apgar scores were not found to be associated with mental disorders," though the authors caution this "may be attributed to incomplete records of Apgar scores during the initial establishment of the Danish Medical Birth Register," and that "the maximum attained age in our study was only up to 39 years," so late-onset disorders (e.g., dementia) could not be detected.

**Context on current guidelines.** "Current guidelines recommend Apgar scores of 7 or higher to be reassuring," but "recent studies showed that even reassuring Apgar scores of 7–9 are associated with higher risks of neonatal mortality, neonatal morbidity, and adverse long-term neurological outcomes, compared with an Apgar score of 10." The authors conclude that "5-min Apgar scores routinely available in contemporary neonatal settings, even within the normal range 7–9, are not totally reassuring."

## Possible explanations offered

The article suggests that "less-than-optimal Apgar scores at birth may be a potential sign of the cumulative effect of those adverse prenatal events," such as "hypoxia-ischemia, white matter injury, reduced blood flow, malnutrition," which "exert a long-lasting impact on brain function in later life." It also notes that "SES factors at least partially mediate the observed association between compromised Apgar scores and neurotic disorder," since individuals with compromised Apgar scores "tended to be born in families with worse SES."

One caveat the authors raise: "a distressed infant will receive resuscitation well before the 5-min Apgar score is assigned, so the score 7–9 could not well reflect severe conditions prior to the assessment."

In short, per this document, the Apgar score is a standard newborn vitality measure, and the study's significance is that even scores in the "normal" 7–9 range are associated with elevated childhood risks of mental and neurodevelopmental disorders, with risk increasing as the score decreases.

Based on the article in `doc.txt`, here is an explanation of the Apgar score and what the study found about its significance for health outcomes.

## What the Apgar score is

The article defines it as follows: "The Apgar score is based on five components (skin color, heart rate, reflex irritability, muscle tone, and respiration). Each item is scored from 0 to 2 with a total score of 7–10 as normal and the highest score of 10 representing the optimal condition" (doc.txt). It is "used worldwide as a vitality index for almost every newborn immediately after birth" (doc.txt).

## The study behind the article

The authors "conducted a population-based cohort study using data from Danish national registers" (doc.txt). "2,272,473 live singletons were identified during 1978–2015 from the Danish Medical Birth Registry" (doc.txt), and "The final cohort comprised 2,213,822 births" (doc.txt).

## Significance for health outcomes

**Even "normal" scores carry some risk.** The main finding is that "individuals with even clinically “normal” Apgar score range of 7–9 still had higher risks of overall mental disorders and some specific diagnoses: organic disorders and a series of neurodevelopmental disorders (intellectual disability, pervasive developmental disorders, childhood autism, and ADHD)" (doc.txt). The authors note a "dose-response increasing the overall risk of mental disorders with decreasing Apgar score of 9 toward 7" (doc.txt).

**Lower scores carry greater risk.** "Compromised Apgar scores were at elevated risks of developing organic disorders and neurotic disorders, which were reported for the first time" (doc.txt). The strongest association was for intellectual disability: the authors "observed 3~5-fold risks of intellectual disability in childhood (until 18 years of age)" (doc.txt), and their findings "further support that compromised 5-min Apgar scores were associated with childhood autism" (doc.txt).

**Early adulthood.** "During early adulthood, compromised 5-min Apgar scores were not found to be associated with mental disorders" (doc.txt), though the authors caution this "may be attributed to incomplete records of Apgar scores during the initial establishment of the Danish Medical Birth Register" (doc.txt), and that "the maximum attained age in our study was only up to 39 years" (doc.txt), so late-onset disorders (e.g., dementia) could not be detected.

**Context on current guidelines.** "Current guidelines recommend Apgar scores of 7 or higher to be reassuring" (doc.txt), but "recent studies showed that even reassuring Apgar scores of 7–9 are associated with higher risks of neonatal mortality, neonatal morbidity, and adverse long-term neurological outcomes, compared with an Apgar score of 10" (doc.txt). The authors conclude that "5-min Apgar scores routinely available in contemporary neonatal settings, even within the normal range 7–9, are not totally reassuring" (doc.txt).

## Possible explanations offered

The article suggests that "less-than-optimal Apgar scores at birth may be a potential sign of the cumulative effect of those adverse prenatal events" (doc.txt), such as "hypoxia-ischemia, white matter injury, reduced blood flow, malnutrition" (doc.txt), which "exert a long-lasting impact on brain function in later life" (doc.txt). It also notes that "SES factors at least partially mediate the observed association between compromised Apgar scores and neurotic disorder" (doc.txt), since individuals with compromised Apgar scores "tended to be born in families with worse SES" (doc.txt).

One caveat the authors raise: "a distressed infant will receive resuscitation well before the 5-min Apgar score is assigned, so the score 7–9 could not well reflect severe conditions prior to the assessment" (doc.txt).

In short, per this document, the Apgar score is a standard newborn vitality measure, and the study's significance is that even scores in the "normal" 7–9 range are associated with elevated childhood risks of mental and neurodevelopmental disorders, with risk increasing as the score decreases.
